title_options: There Are Real Turbines Spinning Inside You 🌀

share.myth: Nothing inside a living cell actually spins like a machine.
share.truth: ATP synthase is a rotary motor: protons flowing through its ring of eight c-subunits (in animals) turn it about 100 times a second; its rotation was first seen directly in 1997 (Watt et al. 2010, PNAS; Noji et al. 1997, Nature).
share.line: Your cells are full of real turbines, spun by protons about a hundred times every second.

facts: Watt IN et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823: the central stalk and c-ring rotate about 100 times per second; the bovine c-ring has 8 subunits, so 8 protons drive one full turn.
Noji H et al. 1997, Nature 386:299: rotation of F1-ATPase seen directly by attaching a fluorescent actin filament to the rotor.
Respiratory chain complexes pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, building the gradient that drives ATP synthase (standard textbooks).
description: Inside your mitochondria, a real rotary motor called ATP synthase is spun by protons about a hundred times a second. Chapter 5 of our book The Tiny Turbine That Powers Your Body. #shorts #biology #science #mitochondria
sources: Watt et al. 2010, PNAS 107:16823 (c8 ring, ~100 rotations per second); Noji et al. 1997, Nature 386:299 (rotation seen directly).

scenes.narration: Inside your cells, a turbine is spinning about a hundred times a second.
It's called ATP synthase, and it sits in the folded inner membrane of your mitochondria.
Tiny pumps in that membrane push protons to one side, like water piling up behind a dam.
The protons flow back through the turbine's ring. In animals, the ring has eight pieces.
Each proton turns the ring one step. Eight protons, one full turn.
In nineteen ninety-seven, scientists in Japan attached a glowing filament to it and watched it rotate.
Your cells are full of real turbines, spun by protons about a hundred times every second.
So what do you think happens to all those turbines when you start to run?
